--- title: "Split-Apply-Combine" error: true --- ## Goals 1. Understand the **split-apply-combine** pattern for analyzing grouped data. 2. Use `groupby` to summarize (`agg`), add group-aware columns (`transform`), and keep or drop whole groups (`filter`). 3. Recognize that **group structure is not always given to you**: groups may have to be constructed from numbers or text, or may be hiding in the data entirely. 4. Appreciate how ignoring group structure can lead to misleading summaries. ## Packages and data ::: {#838e2e4b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import numpy as np import pandas as pd ``` ::: We continue with the Palmer penguins: body measurements for 344 penguins of three species on three islands. ::: {#ed611941 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = pd.read_csv(os.path.join("assets", "penguins.csv")) penguins.isna().sum() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` species 0 island 0 bill_length_mm 2 bill_depth_mm 2 flipper_length_mm 2 body_mass_g 2 sex 11 year 0 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Two rows have *no measurements at all*, and nine more only lack `sex`. We drop the empty rows now and handle `sex` when we need it. (Dropping every row with any missing value would discard information we can use.) ::: {#4fb11973 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = penguins.dropna(subset=["body_mass_g"]) penguins.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (342, 8) ``` ::: ::: ## The split-apply-combine pattern > Many data analysis problems involve the application of a split-apply-combine strategy, where you break up a big problem into manageable pieces, operate on each piece independently and then put all the pieces back together. > > -- Hadley Wickham, [*The Split-Apply-Combine Strategy for Data Analysis*](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v040i01) (2011) - **Split**: divide the data into groups using one or more key variables. - **Apply**: compute something on each group independently (a summary, a transformation, a model). - **Combine**: collect the results into a new table or column. The pattern appears at every stage of an analysis: preparing data (ranking or standardizing *within* groups), summarizing (counts and averages by segment), and modeling (a separate model for each region or customer type). ### Why not just loop? We already know enough to do this by hand: loop over the species, filter the rows, and compute. ::: {#a4f74411 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} for species in sorted(penguins["species"].unique()): subset = penguins[penguins["species"] == species] print(species, round(subset["body_mass_g"].mean(), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adelie 3700.7 Chinstrap 3733.1 Gentoo 5076.0 ``` ::: ::: That works for one number and one grouping variable. But what if we also want the median and the count? What if we group by island too? What if we want the answers in a table we can sort or export? Every change means more bookkeeping code. `groupby` does the splitting, applying, and combining for us. ::: {#fbfd7e42 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].mean().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` species Adelie 3700.7 Chinstrap 3733.1 Gentoo 5076.0 Name: body_mass_g, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ## Splitting ::: {#84904d20 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_species = penguins.groupby("species") by_species ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ``` ::: ::: The `groupby` object *represents* the split. Nothing is computed until we ask for a summary. We can look inside: ::: {#ace35201 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_species.size() # number of rows in each group ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` species Adelie 151 Chinstrap 68 Gentoo 123 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#8b233f1d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} for name, group in by_species: print(name, group.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Adelie (151, 8) Chinstrap (68, 8) Gentoo (123, 8) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a7750be4 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} by_species.get_group("Gentoo").head(3) # pull out one group's rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex year
152 Gentoo Biscoe 46.1 13.2 211.0 4500.0 female 2007
153 Gentoo Biscoe 50.0 16.3 230.0 5700.0 male 2007
154 Gentoo Biscoe 48.7 14.1 210.0 4450.0 female 2007
``` ::: ::: Each group is just a smaller `DataFrame`. Everything we know about tables still works on it. ## Apply and combine ### Aggregation An **aggregation** reduces each group to a few numbers. The `.agg()` method with *named aggregation* lets us choose the output names: each keyword is `new_name=("column", "function")`. ::: {#754baa59 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} mass_summary = ( penguins .groupby("species") .agg( n_penguins=("body_mass_g", "count"), avg_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"), median_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "median"), sd_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "std"), ) .round(1) ) mass_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
n_penguins avg_mass_g median_mass_g sd_mass_g
species
Adelie 151 3700.7 3700.0 458.6
Chinstrap 68 3733.1 3700.0 384.3
Gentoo 123 5076.0 5000.0 504.1
``` ::: ::: Common built-in functions are `"count"`, `"size"`, `"sum"`, `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"std"`, `"min"`, and `"max"`. ::: {.callout-note} ## `count` vs `size` `"count"` counts the **non-missing** values in a column, while `"size"` counts **rows**. They differ when there are missing values: ::: {#d38207f5 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("species")["sex"].agg(["size", "count"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}
size count
species
Adelie 151 146
Chinstrap 68 68
Gentoo 123 119
``` ::: ::: ::: ### Grouping by several keys Pass a list to group by combinations: ::: {#5e35a108 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} species_island = ( penguins .groupby(["species", "island"]) .agg( n_penguins=("body_mass_g", "count"), avg_mass_g=("body_mass_g", "mean"), avg_flipper_mm=("flipper_length_mm", "mean"), ) .round(1) ) species_island ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
n_penguins avg_mass_g avg_flipper_mm
species island
Adelie Biscoe 44 3709.7 188.8
Dream 56 3688.4 189.7
Torgersen 51 3706.4 191.2
Chinstrap Dream 68 3733.1 195.8
Gentoo Biscoe 123 5076.0 217.2
``` ::: ::: The group labels become the **index** of the result (a *multi-level* index here). Use `.reset_index()` to turn them back into ordinary columns: ::: {#ae12f1a7 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} species_island = species_island.reset_index() species_island ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
species island n_penguins avg_mass_g avg_flipper_mm
0 Adelie Biscoe 44 3709.7 188.8
1 Adelie Dream 56 3688.4 189.7
2 Adelie Torgersen 51 3706.4 191.2
3 Chinstrap Dream 68 3733.1 195.8
4 Gentoo Biscoe 123 5076.0 217.2
``` ::: ::: This is usually the right step before exporting, plotting, or merging the table. ::: {#ef4de526 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} species_island.to_csv( os.path.join("output", "species_island_summary.csv"), index = False ) ``` ::: (After `reset_index()` the labels are columns, so `index=False` no longer throws them away. If we had skipped `reset_index()`, `index=False` would have deleted the species and island names from the file.) ### Example: sex differences `sex` has missing values, so we choose to drop those rows *for this question only*. ::: {#5d40e3cd .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} sexed = penguins.dropna(subset=["sex"]) sex_mass = ( sexed .groupby(["species", "sex"])["body_mass_g"] .mean() .unstack("sex") # turn the sex level into columns ) sex_mass["difference"] = sex_mass["male"] - sex_mass["female"] sex_mass.round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
sex female male difference
species
Adelie 3368.8 4043.5 674.7
Chinstrap 3527.2 3939.0 411.8
Gentoo 4679.7 5484.8 805.1
``` ::: ::: `.unstack("sex")` moves one level of the index into the columns, which makes comparisons such as male minus female a simple subtraction. ### Transformation A **transformation** computes a value *for every row*, using information from that row's group. The result has the same number of rows as the original, so it can be stored as a new column. ::: {#66fd7836 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} def zscore(x): """How many standard deviations each value is from the mean.""" return (x - x.mean()) / x.std() penguins["mass_z"] = penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].transform(zscore) penguins[["species", "body_mass_g", "mass_z"]].sample(5, random_state=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
species body_mass_g mass_z
103 Adelie 4250.0 1.197947
126 Adelie 3275.0 -0.928246
12 Adelie 3200.0 -1.091799
249 Gentoo 4875.0 -0.398750
239 Gentoo 5300.0 0.444310
``` ::: ::: - `transform` hands our function each group's column as a `Series`, and expects back a `Series` of the same length. - A `mass_z` of 2 means "two standard deviations heavier than the average *of its own species*". This is a different statement from "heavy compared with all penguins". For common cases you can pass the name of a function: ::: {#fbc0025c .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins["rel_mass"] = ( penguins["body_mass_g"] / penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].transform("mean") ) penguins[["species", "body_mass_g", "rel_mass"]].sample(5, random_state=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
species body_mass_g rel_mass
103 Adelie 4250.0 1.148443
126 Adelie 3275.0 0.884977
12 Adelie 3200.0 0.864710
249 Gentoo 4875.0 0.960399
239 Gentoo 5300.0 1.044126
``` ::: ::: A `rel_mass` of 1.0 means "exactly average for its species". ## Filtering groups `.filter()` keeps or drops *whole groups* based on a condition on the group. Here we keep only species-island combinations with at least 50 penguins: ::: {#0e5bb5d2 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} well_sampled = ( penguins .groupby(["species", "island"]) .filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 50) ) well_sampled.groupby(["species", "island"]).size() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` species island Adelie Dream 56 Torgersen 51 Chinstrap Dream 68 Gentoo Biscoe 123 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: The `lambda g: len(g) >= 50` is a one-line function. It receives each group's sub-table `g` and returns `True` (keep) or `False` (drop). Groups with few observations produce unreliable averages, so a minimum size is a common safeguard. ## Where do groups come from? So far the groups came ready-made: `species`, `island`, and `sex` are columns in the table. This is the easy case. Real data are rarely so convenient, and the most important group structure is often **not labeled**. Groups can arise in four ways: | Source of the groups | Example | Tool | |-------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|------| | 1. Already a column | `species` | `groupby("species")` | | 2. Built from a number | "heavy" vs "light" penguins | `np.where`, `pd.cut`, `pd.qcut` | | 3. Built from text | support tickets sorted into topics | `.str.contains()` + `np.select` | | 4. Hidden in the data | a mixture of groups nobody recorded | *you must notice it* | ::: {.callout-warning} ## Group structure is not always given or obvious Much of the value of an analyst is the ability to *discover* structure that the data do not announce. ::: ### Even labeled groups have traps `groupby` silently ignores rows whose key is missing: ::: {#dbcd972c .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("sex").size() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` sex female 165 male 168 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#dc1003c4 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("sex", dropna=False).size() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` sex female 165 male 168 NaN 9 dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: The first result accounts for fewer penguins than the table contains. Nine rows vanished from the answer without any warning. Always check that your group sizes add up to the number of rows you expect. ### Groups built from numbers To compare "big" and "small" penguins we must first define *big*: ::: {#69f3202b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins["is_big"] = penguins["body_mass_g"] >= 4500 penguins["is_big"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` is_big False 224 True 118 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Averaging a `True`/`False` column gives the **proportion** of `True` values, so we can answer "what share of each species is big?": ::: {#c78fe63f .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("species")["is_big"].mean().round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` species Adelie 0.053 Chinstrap 0.044 Gentoo 0.870 Name: is_big, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: To split a number into several named tiers, use `pd.cut` (you choose the cut points) or `pd.qcut` (cut points chosen so each tier has about the same number of rows): ::: {#b7468637 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins["mass_tier"] = pd.qcut( penguins["body_mass_g"], q=3, labels=["light", "medium", "heavy"] ) penguins["mass_tier"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` mass_tier light 117 heavy 113 medium 112 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#5ecf6ca2 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.crosstab(penguins["species"], penguins["mass_tier"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}
mass_tier light medium heavy
species
Adelie 81 63 7
Chinstrap 36 31 1
Gentoo 0 18 105
``` ::: ::: `pd.crosstab` counts how many rows fall in each combination of two labels. The tiers are *not* spread evenly over species: the constructed groups are tangled up with the labeled ones. ### Groups built from text Suppose we have support tickets, and the only information about the topic is the free-text subject line. ::: {#aa581c48 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} tickets = pd.DataFrame({ "subject": [ "Refund for duplicate charge", "Cannot log in to my account", "Please refund my last order", "Password reset email never arrives", "App crashes when I open it", "Charged twice this month", "Login page shows an error", "App freezes on the checkout screen", "Where is my refund?", "Question about my invoice", "Cannot sign in after the update", "Crash on startup", "Thanks for the great service!", ], "hours_to_resolve": [30, 4, 26, 6, 52, 40, 5, 60, 28, 12, 3, 48, 2], }) ``` ::: There is no `topic` column, so we create one by testing each subject for keywords (see the text notes). `np.select` takes a list of conditions and a list of labels, and picks the label of the first condition that is `True`: ::: {#d7333916 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} subject = tickets["subject"].str.lower() conditions = [ subject.str.contains("refund|charge|invoice"), subject.str.contains("log in|login|sign in|password"), subject.str.contains("crash|freez"), ] labels = ["billing", "access", "app"] tickets["topic"] = np.select(conditions, labels, default="other") tickets[["subject", "topic"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}
subject topic
0 Refund for duplicate charge billing
1 Cannot log in to my account access
2 Please refund my last order billing
3 Password reset email never arrives access
4 App crashes when I open it app
5 Charged twice this month billing
6 Login page shows an error access
7 App freezes on the checkout screen app
8 Where is my refund? billing
9 Question about my invoice billing
10 Cannot sign in after the update access
11 Crash on startup app
12 Thanks for the great service! other
``` ::: ::: Now the usual split-apply-combine works on the group we *created*: ::: {#e0ffca59 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( tickets .groupby("topic") .agg(n_tickets=("subject", "count"), avg_hours=("hours_to_resolve", "mean")) .round(1) .sort_values("avg_hours", ascending=False) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
n_tickets avg_hours
topic
app 3 53.3
billing 5 27.2
access 4 4.5
other 1 2.0
``` ::: ::: Two cautions. First, **the answer depends on our rules**: a different keyword list produces different groups. Second, **always count how many rows landed in `"other"`** and read some of them. If that group is large, the rules are missing something. ### Groups hidden in the data Now the hardest case. Imagine the `species` column had been lost before the data reached you. We would still have the measurements. Could we notice that there are groups? Consider the flipper lengths of all penguins mixed together: ::: {#d2b595c7 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} flipper_counts = pd.cut(penguins["flipper_length_mm"], bins=range(170, 240, 5)).value_counts() flipper_counts.sort_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` flipper_length_mm (170, 175] 2 (175, 180] 11 (180, 185] 28 (185, 190] 58 (190, 195] 57 (195, 200] 38 (200, 205] 18 (205, 210] 30 (210, 215] 33 (215, 220] 32 (220, 225] 20 (225, 230] 14 (230, 235] 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: The counts rise, dip around 200-205 mm, and rise again. A single "typical" flipper length does not describe this population, because there are (at least) two kinds of penguins. If we split at the dip, do we recover real groups? ::: {#c3ab807c .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins["flipper_group"] = np.where( penguins["flipper_length_mm"] >= 206, "long", "short" ) pd.crosstab(penguins["flipper_group"], penguins["species"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}
species Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo
flipper_group
long 2 6 122
short 149 62 1
``` ::: ::: A rule based on a single measurement nearly separates Gentoo from the other two species: almost every "long" penguin is a Gentoo, and almost every Gentoo is "long". The group structure was there all along, and it was visible in the data. ## Bad summary statistics ### Ignoring group structure What if we ignore the groups? Compare the spread of body mass overall with the spread *within* species: ::: {#18e723f6 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("overall sd:", round(penguins["body_mass_g"].std(), 1)) penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].std().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` overall sd: 802.0 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` species Adelie 458.6 Chinstrap 384.3 Gentoo 504.1 Name: body_mass_g, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Much of the overall variation is just the difference *between* species. Labels can also be proxies for something else. Compare average body mass by island, then by island *and* species: ::: {#617e88a7 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby("island")["body_mass_g"].mean().round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` island Biscoe 4716.0 Dream 3713.0 Torgersen 3706.0 Name: body_mass_g, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#ce6e5b89 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.crosstab(penguins["island"], penguins["species"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ```{=html}
species Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo
island
Biscoe 44 0 123
Dream 56 68 0
Torgersen 51 0 0
``` ::: ::: ::: {#f581206f .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins.groupby(["island", "species"])["body_mass_g"].mean().round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ``` island species Biscoe Adelie 3710.0 Gentoo 5076.0 Dream Adelie 3688.0 Chinstrap 3733.0 Torgersen Adelie 3706.0 Name: body_mass_g, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Biscoe penguins look much heavier than Dream or Torgersen penguins. But look at the cross-tabulation: every Gentoo penguin in the data lives on Biscoe, and Gentoo is a large species. Among Adelie penguins, the three islands have almost the same average. The apparent "island effect" is a species effect in disguise. ### Simpson's Paradox For our last example we use `.apply()`, the most general "apply" step. It runs any function on each group's table. Here, the function computes the correlation between bill length and bill depth: ::: {#de1b518c .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} def bill_correlation(g): return g["bill_length_mm"].corr(g["bill_depth_mm"]) overall = penguins["bill_length_mm"].corr(penguins["bill_depth_mm"]) print("all penguins together:", round(overall, 3)) penguins.groupby("species").apply(bill_correlation).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` all penguins together: -0.235 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ``` species Adelie 0.391 Chinstrap 0.654 Gentoo 0.643 dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Taken together, longer bills go with *shallower* bills (negative correlation). Within each species, longer bills go with *deeper* bills (positive). The sign of the relationship flips depending on whether we look at the mixture or at its parts. This phenomenon is known as **Simpson's paradox**. We will revisit this phenomenon in discussing visualization. ::: {.callout-important} ## Takeaway A summary computed over a mixture of groups may describe none of the groups. Before you trust an overall average or correlation, ask: *could there be groups in here that I have not accounted for?* ::: ## Summary | Goal | Code | |--------------------------------------|------| | Summarize by group | `df.groupby("g").agg(name=("col", "mean"))` | | Group by several keys | `df.groupby(["g1", "g2"])` | | Put group labels back into columns | `.reset_index()` | | New column from group statistics | `df.groupby("g")["x"].transform("mean")` | | Keep only some groups | `df.groupby("g").filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 30)` | | Run any function on each group | `df.groupby("g").apply(func)` | | Count combinations | `pd.crosstab(df["a"], df["b"])` | | Create groups from numbers | `np.where`, `pd.cut`, `pd.qcut` | | Create groups from text | `.str.contains()` with `np.select` | | Don't lose rows with missing keys | `groupby(..., dropna=False)` | ## Exercises ### Exercise 1: Summaries 1. Compute the mean `flipper_length_mm` for each species. 2. Compute both the mean and the standard deviation of `bill_length_mm` for each species, in one table. 3. Which species looks largest overall, based on body mass and on flipper length? ### Exercise 2: Two keys Using `species_island`: 1. Which species-island combination has the highest average body mass? Which has the shortest average flipper length? 2. Write 2-3 sentences comparing them. Could the differences be caused by species rather than island? How can you tell? ### Exercise 3: Transformations and filters 1. Using `mass_z`, find the penguins that are more than 2 standard deviations above their species average. How many are there from each island? 2. Change the minimum group size in the filter example from 50 to 30, and then to 60. How many species-island combinations remain each time? ### Exercise 4: Building groups 1. Create a column that splits `bill_length_mm` into three groups with `pd.qcut`. Use `crosstab` to see how the groups line up with species. Do they separate the species as well as the flipper rule did? 2. Treat `species` as a customer segment and `island` as a region. Which segment-region cell has the greatest variability in flipper length? Write 3-4 sentences describing a business situation with the same structure. ### Exercise 5: Hidden structure 1. For body mass vs flipper length, compute the correlation for all penguins together and then for each species. Does the sign flip, as it did for bill measurements? What *does* change? 2. In your own words, explain why an overall correlation can differ from the within-group correlations.
